entries.content:
Thomas Kurian

CEO, Google Cloud

Earlier this month at Gemini at Work, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent for work. It answers your questions, handles your knowledge work, creates your images and media, and writes and runs code. You give it objectives, not instructions, and come back to finished work. It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and has the security, administration, and governance your organization requires.

Every industry runs on knowledge a general model does not have. Government work runs on statute, regulation, and agency guidance, across siloed legacy systems, under strict requirements for data sovereignty, compliance, and confidentiality. Too often that leaves civil servants on data entry and manual document review instead of the services citizens depend on.

Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all.

Five components of Gemini for government services

Developed alongside agency leaders, Gemini for government services provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies with five core components:

  • Skills for government work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Each one applies the statute, regulation, and agency guidance that govern that task, so an agency's standard operating procedures carry into the work Gemini supports.
  • Connectors to agency systems: Secure connectors link Gemini to the case management, ERP, HR, and collaboration systems agencies already run, along with authoritative federal data sources. Gemini queries each system in place, so no data is migrated, and access follows the identity and permission controls the agency already has.
  • Partner agents: Skills and connectors come together in agents, including pre-built agents from public sector software providers that agencies can deploy right away. They handle tasks like FOIA discovery and batch redaction under the same central governance, with a person approving each consequential step.
  • A governed control plane: Security and compliance teams get one place to set and enforce policy across every agent, including VPC Service Controls, CMEK, and Assured Workloads. Outputs are grounded in source documents, with citations, so reviewers can check where each answer came from.
  • An open partner ecosystem: Every agency works under a different statute and runs a different mix of systems. System integrators and public sector ISVs help agencies customize Gemini, connect it to what they already have, and scale it without lock-in.

Skills for government workflows

Gemini for government services helps automate and accelerate complex government operations, including:

  • Policy and regulatory research: Ask an operational or eligibility question and get an answer drawn from the CFR, the Federal Register, state administrative codes, and internal manuals, with page and paragraph citations. Where federal and state rules both apply, Gemini shows which one governs to empower agency decision makers.
  • FOIA record discovery: Gemini searches SharePoint, Drive, and email archives for records responsive to a FOIA or state Sunshine Law request. It organizes them into a review set for the records officer and agency counsel, shortening discovery that often takes weeks.
  • Redaction for public release: Gemini finds sensitive constituent data across a batch of documents, groups the findings so reviewers can clear them in passes, and proposes redactions labeled by statutory exemption. After a reviewer confirms, it produces the exemption log and audit-ready copies.
  • Vendor bid evaluation: Gemini checks multi-volume bids against RFP requirements, FAR guidelines, minimum mandatory criteria, and evaluation rubrics, and returns scoring justifications with citations. Contracting officers get a documented basis for each award decision.
  • Grant and program expense audits: Gemini checks invoices, receipts, purchase orders, and ledger entries against 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance and the terms of the award. It flags unallowable costs, missing documentation, and funding discrepancies with line-item citations, so problems surface while there's still time to fix them.
  • Document validation at intake: Gemini classifies and validates pay stubs, W-2s, utility bills, and leases when they arrive, checks the numbers for consistency, and flags missing signatures. Defects are caught before the application enters the queue, not weeks into the case.
  • Plain-language notices: Gemini turns policy memos and agency guidance into public notices, aligned to the Plain Writing Act of 2010, USDA-FNS standards, and Title VI language access guidance.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the government technology stack

Gemini for government services connects directly to core agency systems via secure connectors. Access is bound by existing role-based access controls, record-level permissions, and the trusted data controls inherited from each system — and nothing is migrated to make the connection work.

Federal regulatory and public data:

  • Federal Register: Tracks legislative actions, regulations, and executive orders as they post, so state and local teams see federal changes as they land.
  • regulations.gov: Tracks federal rulemaking dockets, public comments, and statutory agency response deadlines, keeping policy analysts ahead of incoming mandates.
  • eCFR (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations): Grounds answers in the governing regulation, with citations down to the paragraph.

Agency systems of record:

  • Oracle E-Business Suite: Gives agents permission-bound access to procurement, payables, and ledger transactions for expense auditing and award reconciliation.
  • Oracle PeopleSoft: Connects HR and personnel records under existing role-based controls, so workforce questions are answered from the system of record.
  • Salesforce: Connects constituent case records, service requests, and interaction history, letting agents work a case in context without exporting it.
  • ServiceNow: Automates IT, CRM, security, employee experience, and workflow records, so agents can track incidents, requests, and approval chains inside existing routing rules.

Productivity and collaboration:

  • Google Workspace: Connects with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to analyze case communications and agency correspondence and surface internal files while enforcing agency access controls.
  • Microsoft 365 and SharePoint: Integrates with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint to triage inquiries and ground responses in mail and intranet repositories without breaking workflow context.

Third-party agents and implementation partners

Every agency operates differently. Through our open platform, agencies can deploy pre-built partner agents or work with system integrators to scale custom capabilities:

  • SZNS Solutions FOIA and public records discovery agent: Turns a plain-language request, a piece of correspondence, or a formal citizen inquiry into a scoped search across enterprise archives — bounded by custodian and date range, so a records officer narrows the set before any data moves. It exports responsive material into secure agency repositories and tracks delivery status, giving each request an auditable trail from intake to release.
  • SZNS Solutions document redaction agent: Works inside connected repositories — SharePoint and Drive among them — finding sensitive citizen data across a batch and grouping the findings so a reviewer clears them in passes rather than page by page. Each proposed redaction carries its statutory exemption, and once the reviewer confirms, the agent exports permanently redacted, audit-ready copies back to the system of record, with the processing never leaving the agency's cloud perimeter.
  • Systems integrators & tech partners: Strategic partnerships with Accenture Federal Services, Clutch, Dark Wolf, Daston, Deloitte, Egen, Game Plan Tech, Knexus, Onix, Resultant, SAIC, Slalom, and SZNS Solutions so agencies can customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside federal, state, and local government agencies

We are working closely with select federal and state agencies, including the State of Missouri and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to ensure these capabilities work in day-to-day agency operations.

"Our citizens expect the government to move at the speed of modern life, not the speed of paperwork. By automating routine work in our workflows, we're delivering faster, better services to Missourians." - Tim Marczewski, Director of AI and Innovation, State of Missouri Office of Administration.

Built on an enterprise-grade foundation

Gemini for government services runs on Google Cloud's secure foundation, and can be deployed using the Assured Workloads FedRAMP High Data Boundary, enforcing U.S. data residency and personnel controls. It works within the authorities, retention rules, and approval chains your agency already has.

Agency records, constituent data, institutional documents, custom agents, and model outputs stay private to your organization, and are never used to train or fine-tune Google's foundation models without your permission. Because we operate the full stack, from infrastructure and models through the application layer, we can tune performance and cost together — routing high-volume document parsing and routine records sweeps to fast, low-cost models and reserving high-reasoning models for complex policy analysis, so expanding what your teams can take on does not mean expanding spend at the same rate.

This is just the beginning

The launch of Gemini for government services represents another defining step in delivering on our promise to bring the best of Gemini to every professional, for every workflow, natively tailored to the way they work.

Gemini for government services is available in preview today, joining our purpose-built solutions for industries. We invite leaders at every level of government to explore how Gemini can transform their most critical workflows.

entries.title: Announcements and highlights from Google Public Sector Summit 2026
entries.summary: Today we are bringing together mission leaders and builders from across the public sector at the Google Public Sector Summit in Washington D.C. to explore a critical intersection: Where mission meets moonshot. Through our hands-on programming, we will offer inspiration as well as pragmatic steps for turning moonshot aspirations into secure, scaled, real-world outcomes.From mapping the human genome
entries.content:
Karen Dahut

CEO, Google Public Sector

Today we are bringing together mission leaders and builders from across the public sector at the Google Public Sector Summit in Washington D.C. to explore a critical intersection: Where mission meets moonshot. Through our hands-on programming, we will offer inspiration as well as pragmatic steps for turning moonshot aspirations into secure, scaled, real-world outcomes.

From mapping the human genome to putting a human on the moon, public sector organizations have been at the helm of some of humanity’s most historic breakthroughs. Right now, public sector leaders are being asked to move faster than ever, amidst more complexity and uncertainty, often with fewer resources than the mission demands. To better understand these challenges and opportunities, we surveyed several hundred leaders from across the public sector with theCUBE and ECI Research. According to the findings, while 96.3% of agencies have deployed agents in some form, only 9% have achieved agency-wide adoption. The bottleneck isn’t a lack of vision or ambition—it is the systemic friction of legacy data silos and integration complexity. That is why so many organizations turn to Google; we deliver powerful technology that reduces the toil of getting started, minimizes the friction of integration, and provides the secure foundation for scale.

To that end, we are excited to share several new announcements and capabilities to support your missions and moonshots in the agentic era.

Introducing the Gemini agent

We recently announced the Gemini agent: your new single, universal agent for work. It can have all of your organizational context and can be used for everything from knowledge work to answering questions, and from content creation to coding, all from a single prompt box. At your direction, it can plan the work, use skills and tools, connect to your systems, and bring back something finished — inside the documents, the inbox, and the developer environments you already work in and give it permissions for. With your guidance, the agent chooses the best model for the job, employs built-in cost controls, and most importantly, reflects the security, administration, and governance controls established by your organization.

Introducing Gemini for government services

This morning we launched Gemini for government services in private preview, a purpose-built platform engineered for the security, governance, and workflow complexity of public sector missions. Built around the core promise of delivering "less paperwork, more public service," it provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies. By combining pre-built partner agents, secure connectors, and deterministic skills, the platform enables civil servants to securely link Gemini directly to existing case management, ERP, and agency collaboration systems of record without migrating their agencies’ sensitive data. Civil servants are empowered to automate repetitive, high-stakes tasks—such as public records requests, document intake validation, expense auditing, and policy research—all grounded in authoritative federal regulatory sources with verifiable citations. Learn more about Gemini for government services in our blog post.

Introducing Wiz agents in Wiz for Gov

The Wiz Red, Green, and Blue agents are now available within Wiz for Gov, Wiz’s FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment. The expansion of the agent trio into Wiz for Gov accelerates remediation for critical public sector priorities, including Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The Green Agent can assist in driving PQC readiness through a new risk type dedicated to weak cryptography that investigates whether an asset is quantum-vulnerable and assesses potential Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) exposure. By leveraging the cryptographic visibility from code to runtime gained through the Wiz AI-APP, the Wiz Green Agent is able to help weigh real-world external reachability against data sensitivity enabling delivery of continuously updated, PQC-resistant fixes directly into developer workflows.

Wiz has also invested in several other initiatives intended to benefit the public sector. Scan for Good, a program launched jointly by Wiz and Google DeepMind, uses the Wiz Red Agent and Gemini 4 Argon, alongside Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, to provide no-cost security assessments designed to uncover high-risk vulnerabilities and exposures across eligible public services, critical infrastructure, and other under-resourced organizations. Wiz is also expanding capabilities for organizations navigating the new FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rulesets. This includes operationalizing critical FedRAMP metrics, including Potential Agency Impact (PAIN), and validating likely exploitability (LEV) and internet reachability (IRV). These enhancements will assist organizations seeking to achieve or maintain FedRAMP certification with the automated reporting and prioritized risk assessment required.

Bringing enterprise search capabilities to Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud

For defense, intelligence, and national security agencies operating in classified environments, the challenge is not just analyzing vast volumes of sensitive data, it is doing so without compromising perimeter security. To help turn classified information into actionable intelligence, we are bringing enterprise search capabilities to Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud for air-gapped deployments. With this new capability, users gain an intuitive conversational interface to query, synthesize, and summarize records at machine speed, completely disconnected from the public internet. This launch brings Gemini 3.5 Flash models to on-premises air-gapped deployments, expands model flexibility with open models like Gemma, and delivers massive local compute through generally available NVIDIA Blackwell B300 GPUs.

Driving mission impact, together

Through partnership and powerful technology, organizations across the public sector are transforming how services are delivered, accelerating research and science, strengthening national security, improving healthcare delivery, and enhancing student outcomes. These organizations aren’t waiting for the future; they are actively building it right now.

  • America.gov is offering a streamlined "front door" that simplifies access to federal services online. Google is proud to be named a technology partner in this vital initiative, leveraging Gemini to help millions of Americans access critical public resources with greater speed and ease.
  • SUNY is tackling challenges with direct impact for communities across New York and beyond. Together, we are ​​empowering researchers of all technical backgrounds to easily access and benefit from Google Cloud's advanced capabilities—bringing storage, high-powered computing, Gemini Enterprise, and more than 200 trusted models together into a seamless, centralized ecosystem.
  • The Department of Energy is accelerating breakthroughs in energy dominance, discovery science, and national security through the Genesis Mission. Gemini will support the full breadth of work - from the research bench to specialized user facilities – building a secure foundation that the DOE mission can depend on.
  • The U.S. Army is leading a sweeping modernization of its logistics infrastructure including non-tactical logistics networks, supply chain procedures, and organic industrial base sites. The Army's Strategic Capital Initiative will pair Google's secure cloud and FedEx's logistics expertise to build a more intelligent and connected supply chain network that helps reduce delivery times and ensures personnel receive the critical equipment where and when they need it.
  • The Department of War is supercharging daily operations and workflows with Gemini, giving 3 million personnel across the department access to a secure enterprise-grade platform. With Agent Designer, GenAI.mil users are quickly able to build their own agents using natural language to help streamline repetitive, multi-step tasks such as document creation and document reviews.
  • Case Western Reserve University is improving learning outcomes and accelerating research breakthroughs. They are leveraging Gemini for education campus-wide, transforming the experience of every scientist, staff member, and student. Tomorrow, they’re opening a new hub for discovery and innovation that leverages Google technology, and connects Google engineers with 300 university researchers across campus.

Google Public Sector: Your mission partner

The agentic era will not be defined by what technology can do, but by what we choose to build with it. So let’s meet this moment, let's re-imagine what’s possible, and let’s create impact — together.

  • Register early for Google Public Sector Summit On-Demand to be notified when the event’s content is published.
  • Learn how Gemini for government services can help transform critical workflows and advance your mission.
  • Request a demo to see how the Wiz Agents can help your agency meet today’s security demands at machine speed.
  • Catch the highlights from Google Public Sector Summit on our Linkedin page, schedule a 1:1 consultation with a Google team member or reach us at geminiforgov@google.com.

entries.title: Managed RAG search inside the sovereign perimeter: Gemini on GDC enterprise search
entries.summary: National security agencies and other sovereign and highly regulated organizations handle incredibly sensitive data such as classified reports, field manuals, and sensitive multi-modal datasets. Search and multimodal intelligence that’s available in the public cloud can help teams manage and analyze that data, but due to strict data sovereignty mandates, that data cannot leave the customer premises
entries.content:
Rohan Grover

Senior Director, Google Distributed Cloud

National security agencies and other sovereign and highly regulated organizations handle incredibly sensitive data such as classified reports, field manuals, and sensitive multi-modal datasets. Search and multimodal intelligence that’s available in the public cloud can help teams manage and analyze that data, but due to strict data sovereignty mandates, that data cannot leave the customer premises.

The alternative has been to deploy custom agentic search inside a secure, disconnected perimeter, but until now, that meant months building and maintaining custom infrastructure — stitching together models, building speech-to-text and optical character recognition (OCR) pipelines, configuring vector databases, and managing a bespoke user interface.

Today, we're excited to announce enterprise search capabilities with Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped to help solve the above challenges. In preview, this fully managed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) search experience runs entirely inside your physical security perimeter, with no connection to the public internet or to Google Cloud's global infrastructure. Your teams can now upload their files into a conversation and ask Gemini to find information about it, summarize it, compare it, or translate it. Every answer cites its sources, and conversations persist between sessions.

Enterprise search capabilities on GDC enable your teams to search across siloed data and unlock powerful insights. With these capabilities, you can now:

  • Go from hundreds of pages to a cited answer: Ask questions across long manuals, reports, and policies, and see exactly which files each answer came from.
  • Work across languages: Ask in one language and get answers grounded in documents written in another, or have Gemini translate them.
  • Ask one question across many formats: Combine audio recordings, video clips, images, and spreadsheets with no separate transcription or OCR steps.
  • Pick up where you left off: Conversations and files persist between sessions, so you don’t have to start from scratch on long-running work.
  • Keep access need-to-know: Each user's chats and files are private to that user, and access follows the identity provider groups you already manage.

Users can work with PDF, Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, plus TXT, HTML, PNG and JPEG images, WAV audio, and MP4 video. Each file can be up to 100 MB, and each chat up to 500 MB.

Core architectural layers: under the hood

Let's follow a user query through each layer of the stack: signing in, ingesting files, generating the response with Gemini, and storing the session. Every step happens on the organization's air-gapped network.

Identity and access

Users sign in through their organization's identity provider. Administrators map the service's user role to identity provider groups, and only members of those groups can access the application. Each user's chats and uploaded files are private to that user.

Document ingestion and embedding

When a user uploads a file, it goes straight to the app's object storage bucket. The backend records the file's metadata in the app's managed PostgreSQL database, which is optimized for search. The backend then splits the file into chunks, such as groups of PDF pages or tiles of an image, and writes them to the bucket. A Gemini embedding model running natively within the GDC deployment converts each chunk into a vector, which the backend stores in the app's PostgreSQL database.

When the user asks a question, the state-of-the-art (SOTA) Gemini model running entirely on GDC inside the customer’s data center first rewrites the question with context from the conversation. The backend then embeds the rewritten question with the same model and searches the vector database.

Model serving

The backend then combines the question, the conversation history, and the best-matching data into a single multimodal prompt and sends it to a Gemini endpoint running on NVIDIA B300 GPUs in that same GDC deployment. Gemini is natively multimodal — it accepts text, images, audio, and video as input, so it can reason across data coming from different file types in a single context, and doesn't require separate speech-to-text and OCR models. The answer then streams back to the user with citations to the source files.

Persistence

Lastly, the persistence layer keeps each conversation's state. Each question and answer is stored in the system’s database and uploaded files stay in object storage, so users can reopen an earlier session and pick up where they left off.

Built for classified and sovereign environments

With Gemini and enterprise search on GDC, prompts, responses, uploaded documents, and embeddings never leave your organization's air-gapped network, and every model runs locally. Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 disk encryption using locally managed HSM keys, and in transit with TLS using FIPS-approved algorithms. Local IAM integration with granular role-based access control (RBAC) governs access to resources. GDC air-gapped has U.S. DoD IL6 accreditation and is designed to support strict requirements in alignment with FedRAMP High security controls.

Code execution: Compliance and security

To deliver precise, deterministic answers from structured spreadsheet data (such as CSV and XLSX files), Gemini enterprise search leverages the Gemini inference stack's local code-execution engine.

When handling analytical queries — such as computing the average salary across departments — Gemini dynamically generates Python code and runs it securely within Agent Substrate, an open-source execution runtime built for large-scale agent orchestration.

To mitigate security risks inherent to executing LLM-generated code, Agent Substrate enforces strict network isolation and runs workloads inside gVisor sandboxes, helping ensure strong isolation boundaries without sacrificing inference performance.

Bringing frontier models to the sovereign data center

You no longer have to choose between uncompromising security and cutting-edge multimodal intelligence. Enterprise search, Gemini 3.5 Flash and databases optimized for search run together inside the GDC air-gapped perimeter with no dependency on the internet to bring the best autonomous capabilities to the sovereign cloud.

Explore the GDC air-gapped documentation and contact your GDC representative to learn how you can best leverage these search capabilities in your sovereign cloud.

entries.title: Enabling the next era of sovereign AI: The latest Google Distributed Cloud innovations
entries.summary: Agentic systems are quickly moving from pilots to production in the enterprise. But if your organization operates under stringent data sovereignty, defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure mandates, sending sensitive data to a public cloud often isn’t an option — and building your own AI stack inside a disconnected perimeter can take months. Your missions demand frontier models, hardened
entries.content:
Muninder Sambi

VP, Product Management & Supply Chain, Google Distributed Cloud

Agentic systems are quickly moving from pilots to production in the enterprise. But if your organization operates under stringent data sovereignty, defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure mandates, sending sensitive data to a public cloud often isn’t an option — and building your own AI stack inside a disconnected perimeter can take months. Your missions demand frontier models, hardened security, and high performance, deployed directly where your most sensitive data lives.

The latest innovations in Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped represent a huge leap forward for organizations struggling with these challenges, and they no longer need to make this tradeoff. Enterprise search capabilities with Gemini, support for open weight models, turnkey ISV applications, next-generation accelerated infrastructure, and support for new partners are all now available to be directly deployed in your sovereign, air-gapped environments.

Here’s a high-level look at the major capabilities launching across three pillars: Sovereign AI and enterprise search, next-generation infrastructure, and a growing ISV partner ecosystem.

GDC technology stack: Infra, frontier models, data and applications

The GDC technology stack turns isolated infrastructure into a modern agentic innovation platform, combining foundational and open model flexibility, intuitive out-of-the-box user experiences, and high-performance data processing.

Overview of GDC architecture and capabilities

We are excited to bring the following innovations to GDC:

  • Gemini on GDC enterprise search: In air-gapped environments, analysts and knowledge workers spend critical hours manually sifting through compartmentalized documents, intercepted audio, and sensor video. Agentic systems can streamline those processes, but building those capabilities often requires months of custom development. With enterprise search capabilities in Gemini on GDC (available in preview), organizations gain a turnkey conversational interface, so they can query, prompt, and summarize vast repositories of data near-instantaneously. Unlike text-only open-source alternatives, this managed architecture delivers native multi-modality support via Gemini embedding models, combining high-throughput scaling and low-latency inference performance for text, audio, and video modalities. Built-in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) keeps indexing and interactions strictly within your sovereign perimeter, accelerating insights without compromising security.
  • Expanded frontier and open-weight models: Google Cloud is one of the first hyperscalers to bring a frontier model like Gemini to air-gapped deployments. Now generally available on GDC air-gapped, Gemini 3.5 Flash delivers ultra-low-latency reasoning, multimodal understanding, and long-context capabilities entirely within your air-gapped boundary, allowing users to process large volumes of field intelligence, from reports to imagery and recordings, quickly. GDC also now supports leading open models like Gemma and Mistral, giving you architectural and workload choice, giving you the flexibility to match the right model to each workload on the same governed platform.

Next-generation IaaS powering GDC

To run modern agentic systems and memory-intensive enterprise workloads on the same infrastructure, you need an uncompromising foundation. GDC air-gapped features a new, elevated Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) stack across compute, networking, and security, so you can run AI and traditional workloads side by side with the performance and protection they need.

  • Next-gen high-performance agentic infrastructure: NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture are now generally available on GDC air-gapped, giving you the local compute to serve Gemini and open models — and the agents built on them — at production scale. Paired with VM networking that now supports up to 32 Gbps per VM (up from 25 Gbps), you can move data to your GPUs faster and reduce bottlenecks in your inference pipelines.
  • Resilient, enterprise-grade networking: Fully managed Cloud DNS, now generally available on GDC, lets your platform teams manage DNS records with the same Kubernetes APIs and command line they already use — with no third-party DNS infrastructure to deploy, patch, and maintain inside the air gap. And hardware-offloaded IPsec encryption protects node-to-node traffic at up to 100 Gbps, helping you meet encryption-in-transit requirements without taking CPU away from your applications.
  • SecOps enabled by Elastic: As agentic workloads scale, you need machine-speed security to defend your distributed environments. Through our deep integration with Elastic Security, we are modernizing threat detection and response (SIEM and EDR) on GDC air-gapped. Together, Elastic Security and GDC air-gapped provide automated case management, behavioral analytics, and agentic-driven telemetry correlation, so you can accelerate your mean time to response (MTTR).

Expanding the sovereign ISV partner ecosystem

Your missions depend on more than infrastructure — they run on the data platforms, developer tools, and collaboration apps your teams already know. That’s why we’re bringing more of that software to run natively on GDC, so you can adopt AI without leaving familiar tools behind. Today, we’re expanding the GDC partner marketplace with independent software vendors (ISVs) including Teradata, Solo.io, and Mattermost:

  • Teradata extends industry-standard enterprise data analytics and warehouse intelligence to the distributed edge, so you can run complex analytical pipelines right next to local AI inference — and act on insights without moving data outside your perimeter.

"Enterprises in highly regulated and air-gapped environments are eager to harness the transformative power of generative AI, but they cannot compromise on data privacy or analytical rigor. By bringing Teradata to Google Distributed Cloud, we are enabling our joint customers to run complex analytical workloads and AI inferencing right where their data resides. Together with Google Cloud, we are breaking down barriers between sovereign cloud infrastructure and enterprise-grade intelligence." - Sumeet Arora, Chief Product Officer, Teradata

  • Solo.io brings API management, service mesh, and agentic networking — including kagent and agentgateway — to sovereign deployments, so you can securely connect and govern microservices and AI agents across isolated clusters, including which tools and other agents each agent can reach.
  • Mattermost delivers secure collaboration and mission-critical operations workflows for defense and public sector teams, so your people can coordinate in real time entirely inside the air gap — including AI-assisted summaries and translation using models running locally on GDC.

Building the future of sovereign cloud

With these capabilities, sovereignty no longer has to slow down your AI ambitions. By bringing Gemini and open-weight models, multimodal enterprise search, high-performance infrastructure, built-in security, and a growing ISV ecosystem together inside your air-gapped perimeter, GDC helps you turn your most sensitive data into actionable insights, while you maintain compliance, security, and control.

Ready to get started?

  • Read our technical deep dive on Gemini on GDC enterprise search.
  • Explore the GDC air-gapped documentation.
  • Contact your GDC representative to schedule a demo.

entries.title: Building full virtual vehicles on Google Cloud: From AAOS to the smallest MCU
entries.summary: Imagining traditional gearheads getting their hands on software-defined vehicles is an amusing thought experiment. With their socket wrenches and air compressors at the ready, they might be confused to encounter core functions more likely to run on 1s and 0s than oil and belts. But across the auto industry these days, more and more vehicles feature prominent systems built using cloud-native develo
entries.content:
Florian Haubner

Industry Architect Lead Automotive

Per Sigurdson

CEO & co-founder, RemotiveLabs

Imagining traditional gearheads getting their hands on software-defined vehicles is an amusing thought experiment. With their socket wrenches and air compressors at the ready, they might be confused to encounter core functions more likely to run on 1s and 0s than oil and belts. But across the auto industry these days, more and more vehicles feature prominent systems built using cloud-native development, continuous integration/continuous delivery, fast digital iteration, and plenty of AI.

But there’s still a big gap to be found in many automakers’ and Tier 1 suppliers’ cloud-based development processes. On the one hand, these companies are commonly using software to develop vehicles’ digital entertainment and information screens, or other onboard high-performance computers.

On the other, the dozens of microchips and control modules that make a car a car these days — such as gateways, body controllers, zone control units, sensor and actuator nodes — are still frequently hardwired to physical chips when they’re constructed, making them very difficult to update, reprogram, or expand after the vehicle drives off the factory floor. Teams have to wait for benches, samples, and rigs, and integration can easily slip to the end of the development process, where defects are most expensive to fix.

This inherent inefficiency has become a leading bottleneck. After all, manufacturers can’t really claim vehicles are software-defined if most of their electronics only function when connected to physical hardware and if developers are leaning heavily on actual hardware.

With Horizon, our agentic innovation platform for developing software-defined vehicles, our vision is to help manufacturers avoid these inefficiencies by working with partners like RemotiveLabs.

The cockpit already runs in the cloud

The Android team has invested a significant amount of time and effort over the last few years on enabling seamless development of the many digital systems in vehicles’ cockpits. Android Automotive OS (AAOS) runs inside Google’s official virtual testing environment for Android, Cuttlefish, which itself runs comfortably on Arm-based Google Cloud instances. With this approach, developers can build, boot, and test virtual versions of their infotainment stacks on the same Arm architecture that ships in vehicles.

And with the recent launch of Android 17 and AAOS SDV, this capability is also extended to further domains, whenever AAOS SDV is used. Deploying it with Cuttlefish, for example, proves the model: representative software, on representative architecture, in the cloud, on demand. The question that still needs to be answered is how to extend that model to the rest of the vehicle, especially when other operating systems are involved.

The harness around the virtual vehicle

That’s where RemotiveTopology comes into play. As the harness around the virtual vehicle, it’s the layer that connects AAOS in Cuttlefish to a full, simulated electrical and electronic (E/E) architecture: the rest of the vehicle’s onboard computers, its data networks, and the live signals that make the system function like a real vehicle rather than a collection of standalone apps.

RemotiveTopology automatically utilizes manufacturers’ existing network design files to build a working, virtual version of their cars’ networks. This is vehicle-as-code: the E/E architecture expressed as an executable specification, versioned and provisioned like infrastructure-as-code. In this way, an entire vehicle can be spun up on demand. Cockpit software talks to the rest of the vehicle exactly as it would in a real vehicle. As a result, developers get full and continuous signal and cross-domain visibility, so they can see real-time system status. And because it is built on standard Linux tooling, the same topology runs on a laptop and in a contiguous integration pipeline on Google Cloud.

Integrate across domains early, not late

The payoff for using this approach is that all onboard systems can be developed and integrated with software before any of them are connected to a vehicle’s hardware. That’s beneficial because the most difficult (and latest) integration in a vehicle’s development is bringing all its systems together. For example, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) produce object lists, trajectories, and mode requests that the cockpit has to render and react to, while the infotainment system and information cluster have to reflect driving state while body and chassis nodes sit in the loop.

With the full topology live on Google Cloud, the infotainment system and ADAS can operate simultaneously within a virtual vehicle, exchanging real signals over the simulated network. This means it’s possible to exercise handoffs like an ADAS event surfacing in the cluster or a driver-mode change rippling across domains from day one in continuous integration long before the benches and samples line up. In this way, developers can be confident they’ll discover multi-domain integration long before the end of the process so that they can test continuously from the start.

The full vehicle frontier

At the heart of this work is a shared desire to bring scalable software development to even the smallest and most common nodes in a vehicle, its microchips and control modules. That’s because these are the parts that have traditionally been wired to hardware, and as a result are the biggest blocker to fully software-defined vehicles.

The ultimate goal is that the same software that runs in the cloud can run on vehicles’ actual control modules with no re-tooling or re-validation needed to move between them. That parity is natural with Arm-based Google Cloud infrastructure because the cloud and the car share an instruction set. Google's Axion makes it straightforward: C4A metal, a bare-metal Arm instance, is provided explicitly for automotive systems development and Android software development, giving direct hardware access without unnecessary software layers and delivering the consistent performance that vehicle systems require.

Taken together, this holistic system allows teams, for the first time, to develop and integration-test an entire vehicle’s systems in the cloud and then apply it to the actual vehicle without having to rewrite it.

Why now, and where to start

The payoff is not abstract. Treating the vehicle as code and moving integration into the cloud compresses the slowest, most expensive phase of a program. Early customer engagements with RemotiveLabs have measured more than 10x faster integration cycles. And the development loop is now changing faster than the hardware loop: AI-assisted and agentic workflows can rapidly generate, test, and refine vehicle software, but only virtual systems provide the required scale. Every element that can’t be virtualized can slow the entire development process down.

RemotiveTopology provides this architecture as vehicle-as-code and makes it accessible for developers, testers, and autonomous AI agents alike. Best of all, there is no new third-party tooling to adopt just to get started. Instead, RemotiveLabs publishes an open-source simplified vehicle on GitHub that anyone can run in minutes on standard Linux tooling and platform definitions already in place. Full existing toolchains plug in as a manufacturer or Tier1 supplier scales, and RemotiveTopology can be easily dropped into an Arm-based Google Cloud environment.

For those building software-defined vehicles whose virtual development stops at the cockpit, it’s time to start with an open-source example, bring unique platform definitions, and run an entire vehicle in the cloud. RemotiveTopology is available in Horizon for easy usage in combination with other Horizon modules.

While UDF logging enables a wide range of operational monitoring and debugging workflows
entries.content:
Cong Du

Software Engineer

Ming Ma

Software Engineer

We are announcing  a new logging feature that  is now available in Python User-Defined Function (UDF) in BigQuery. Developers can now use Python’s standard logging library directly inside BigQuery UDFs to emit structured logs seamlessly into Cloud Logging—with zero external plugins or custom connectors required.

While UDF logging enables a wide range of operational monitoring and debugging workflows, to demonstrate this feature we are showcasing an example for building fault-tolerant, resilient data pipelines. In the example below, we are capturing row-level diagnostic telemetry during query execution, so that teams can easily isolate problematic records, trigger real-time alerts, and triage issues via SQL without halting entire workloads.

In this post, we’ll show you how to get started with Python UDF logging and walk through an e-commerce event ingestion pipeline as a practical, end-to-end example.

Architecture overview

The workflow consists of three stages:

  • Inline validation: The Python UDF parses incoming JSON payloads. Valid records pass to the destination table; corrupted or non-compliant rows trigger 

    logging.error()
    and return 
    NULL
    to prevent query failure.

  • Real-time alerting: A Cloud Monitoring log-based metric notifies your team when error rates breach SLA thresholds.

  • SQL triage & replay: Data engineers query the quarantined payloads in BigQuery using standard SQL over the linked 

    _AllLogs
    view, diagnose the root cause, and re-ingest recovered data.

Although this specific demonstration relies on Python for data validation and transformation, you can seamlessly integrate Python-driven logging and validation into pipelines that perform SQL-based transformations.

Quickstart walkthrough: Step-by-step

Step 1: Create the generic Python UDF

This UDF parses JSON and checks for a required field. If parsing fails or the required key is missing, it logs structured diagnostic JSON and returns 

NULL
.

Step 2: Run ingestion with logging enabled

In this example, we simulate an e-commerce event ingestion pipeline processing incoming user actions (

click
, 
view
, 
checkout
). Our goal is to extract valid events into our clean analytics table while gracefully quarantining broken or missing-schema payloads.

Enable logging in your session with 

SET @@udf.properties
:

Ingestion Results

The query succeeds without interruption while bad rows (2 and 3) are routed to Cloud Logging.

Step 3: Set up real-time alerts on Cloud Logging

You can configure alerts to notify your on-call team as soon as malformed payloads exceed acceptable thresholds.

In the Google Cloud Console (1-Click)

  • In the Google Cloud Console, open Logs Explorer.

  • Paste the log filter for your UDF routine:

3. Click Create alert in the top action bar.

4. Set your notification channels (e.g., Slack, PagerDuty, or Email) and save the policy.

Step 4: Triage bad rows with BigQuery Log Analytics

"Note: To query your logs via BigQuery SQL, ensure you have enabled BigQuery Log Analytics on your Cloud Logging bucket and created a linked dataset."

Query the quarantined payloads using BigQuery SQL via the linked 

_AllLogs
view:

Log Analytics output

Recovering data

Because full raw payloads are preserved in Cloud Logging, you can recover quarantined records directly with SQL once upstream data is fixed:

Final 
clean_events
Table Result:

All valid and recovered data is now unified in the production table without any data loss.

Other use cases

  • Shadow execution & safe migrations: Run legacy and new business logic side-by-side in a UDF. Return the legacy result to production while logging calculation differences to Cloud Logging.

  • PII redaction auditing: Mask sensitive tokens (such as SSNs or account numbers) before writing to BigQuery, while emitting anonymized audit events to Cloud Logging.

  • ML inference drift: Log warnings when embedded scoring logic encounters out-of-vocabulary inputs or low model confidence.

Best practices

  • Enable debug output: Include 

    SET @@udf.properties = JSON '{"enableDebugOutput": true}';
    in the session where you want logs captured.

  • Avoid sensitive data in logs: Cloud Logging is visible to users with Logging Viewer permissions. Do not log credentials or secrets.

  • Cost management: On high-throughput pipelines, log selectively (e.g., only on errors or via sampling) to manage logging ingestion volume.

entries.title: Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators
entries.summary: Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective? There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases: Verbosity bias: LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers, even when the underlying facts are wrong. Position bias: Swapping
entries.content:
Héctor González Álvarez

Senior Technical Solutions Consultant, Google Cloud

Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective?

There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases:

  • Verbosity bias: LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers, even when the underlying facts are wrong.
  • Position bias: Swapping the order of two options can cause an LLM judge to flip its verdict over 75% of the time.
  • The halo effect: Because LLMs generate text piece by piece, clean grammar and formatting can trick an AI judge into giving top marks for accuracy while missing errors.
  • Agreeableness bias: LLM judges are great at recognizing valid work. But with detecting errors, they may fail to catch incorrect, buggy, or unsafe outputs up to 75% of the time.
  • Self-enhancement bias: Also known as egocentric bias, AI evaluators systematically overrate outputs that were generated by themselves or from their own family.

Ultimately, LLM judges are not objective arbiters of truth. They are subjective models with their own distinct biases. Treating them as infallible tools that don't need their quality measured might leave your work compromised.

In this post, we’ll explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality.

Three helpful ways to audit your LLM judges

Pillar 1: Measure internal stability

Before you can trust an AI judge’s score, you need to know that it isn't just guessing. Because LLMs are probabilistic, they can be inconsistent, giving different scores to the exact same text.

You can test this internal stability by running multi-pass consistency checks on a single output and calculating the variance. If a judge's scores fluctuate wildly on identical inputs, its rubric is too ambiguous.

Pillar 2: Validate human alignment

When your evaluation datasets are mostly valid responses, a lenient AI judge can look great on paper. It might align closely with human reviewers overall, but miss a majority of invalid or even unsafe outputs.

To prove your LLM judge is catching real errors, you need chance-corrected metrics. These mathematical models filter out agreements driven purely by leniency or random chance, showing how closely your evaluator actually aligns with the informed decisions of human experts.

Pillar 3: Use multi-judge ensembles

To avoid the halo effect mentioned earlier, teams should use decomposed prompting. Instead of asking one LLM judge to score an entire response, assign a specialized judge to evaluate a single criteria, like factual accuracy or tone. This isolates traits and forces independent scoring.

Second, to track performance in real time without human intervention, the established best practice is ensembling. This means running at least two different models under the hood to evaluate the exact same output simultaneously.

By finding the statistical consensus between these models, you can flag if their evaluations begin to diverge and avoid any scoring quality degradation.

Get started

Partner with Delta to design and implement statistically-audited evaluation pipelines for your enterprise agentic systems.

entries.content:
Dave Wang

Forward Deployed Engineer, Google Cloud

Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn.

MCP Apps (SEP-1865) solves this. This open Model Context Protocol (MCP) extension pairs a tool with a live UI. In Gemini Enterprise, that UI renders directly in the chat flow inside a sandboxed iframe, and can expand to fullscreen or a side panel. Edits run locally while the workspace and assistant stay synchronized.

You also avoid rebuilding core foundations: Gemini provides workforce sign-in, governed data access, and the Default Assistant, while you host your MCP server on a private Cloud Run service.

Why we need MCP Apps

Enterprise assistants have evolved through three generations:

  • Generation 1 (Text chatbots): Returns static markdown with no interactive controls.

  • Generation 2 (Standard MCP tools): Invokes live APIs, but outputs static text. Every change requires another model turn.

  • Generation 3 (Interactive MCP Apps): Pairs each tool with a live workspace. Adjustments happen in the widget without a model turn, while the assistant stays in sync.

Building MCP Apps in Gemini delivers six benefits:

  • Responsive user experience: Single-click actions execute directly in the panel without round-tripping through the chat.

  • Purpose-built workflows: Deliver visual redaction views for legal review, 3D viewers for CAD, or sensitivity models for finance.

  • Enterprise security: Workforce OAuth sign-in, private Cloud Run ingress, and a sandboxed iframe protect every layer.

  • Human-in-the-loop governance: Experts inspect and approve high-stakes actions before execution.

  • Open standard: Portable across compatible hosts, with automatic text fallback.

  • Broad connectivity: Connect to BigQuery, Agent Platform, Cloud Storage, or internal ERP and CRM systems.

High-level architecture

Three decoupled tiers work together:

  • Client browser: Shows the chat alongside the MCP App widget in the side panel.

  • Gemini Enterprise: The default assistant calls tools, the AppBridge proxy relays widget messages, and the connector manages OAuth.

  • Google Cloud (your project): You deploy and host the MCP server on Cloud Run, which exposes one JSON-RPC endpoint (/mcp), runs background jobs, and serves the single-file HTML widget.

Each tier talks only to its neighbor, letting Gemini Enterprise enforce security and routing.

Authentication with two independent layers

Each user signs in through OAuth 2.0. On every call, Gemini Enterprise sends its service agent token alongside the user's OAuth token:

  • Layer 1 (Cloud Run IAM): Enforced at Google's edge, this answers "which service may call?" Public access is disabled; unauthorized callers receive HTTP 403.

  • Layer 2 (In-App OAuth): Enforced inside the application, this answers "which user is calling?" Failed verification returns HTTP 401, prompting the user to sign in again.

Cloud Run IAM cannot distinguish end users, so both layers are required. Outbound calls use a least-privilege service account.

Build, deploy on Google Cloud, and register in Gemini Enterprise

First, build your custom MCP server (exposing POST /mcp and a bundled ui:// HTML widget) using the MCP Apps SDK, or use Google Antigravity  to scaffold and deploy your MCP App with this starter prompt:

  • Build an MCP App for Gemini Enterprise using the create-mcp-app skill (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/tree/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-mcp-app).

  • Workflow: [describe your input data, side-panel UI controls, and approval or export actions].

  • Generate a single-file HTML widget, a Streamable HTTP backend (POST /mcp) with <2s async tool responses and get_app_state polling, and Cloud Run deployment commands (--no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling, --min-instances=1).

Once your MCP server code is ready, deploy it to Cloud Run and connect it to Gemini Enterprise:

  • Step 1: Enable APIs for Cloud Run, Discovery Engine, Agent Platform, and Organization Policy.

  • Step 2: Deploy your MCP server container to Cloud Run from source 

    (gcloud run deploy  --source .
    ) with 
    --no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling
    so background work does not freeze between polls, and --min-instances=1.

  • Step 3: Grant the invoker role (

    roles/run.invoker
    ) to your Discovery Engine service agent (Layer 1).
  • Step 4: Create an OAuth 2.0 Web Client with redirect URI 
    https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect
    (Layer 2).

  • Step 5: Override the 

    discoveryengine.managed.disableCustomMcpServerConnector
    constraint and complete the Before you begin prerequisites 
    (roles/discoveryengine.editor
    for the admin, allowedEgressFqdns for your server and OAuth hosts, and 
    custom_mcp
    in 
    allowedDataSources
    if enforced). Then, in the Google Cloud Console under Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > Create data store, select Custom MCP Server and register the connector:

  • Step 6: Enable actions on your data store. Gemini Enterprise imports your MCP server's tools as actions and disables them by default. In the Cloud Console, open Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > [Your MCP Data Store] > Actions, click Reload custom actions (which calls 

    tools/list
    on your server), select your model-visible tools, and click Enable actions.
  • Step 7: Connect the data store to your app. Open Gemini Enterprise > Apps > [Your App] > Connected data stores > Add existing data stores, and select your MCP data store. Connecting it as a data store gives the built-in Default Assistant access to your MCP tools and UI widget directly in main chat ( do not use "Add Agent,"  which is for external sub-agents rather than MCP data stores).

Build your own

An MCP App pairs backend tools with a live workspace in Gemini Enterprise. You do not build a chat frontend or identity pipeline; you deploy one Cloud Run container and attach it as a Data Store, making Gemini Enterprise where enterprise work gets done.

  • Try Gemini here

  • Co-build with Google Antigravity here

  • Build on Google Cloud: MCP Apps Specification (SEP-1865), Cloud Run, and Google Cloud AI.

entries.title: Google named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms
entries.summary: As organizations work to leverage AI to transform their businesses, it is clear that the raw model intelligence is not the key challenge.Consistently, we hear that the challenges lie in how the agents can be deployed across the company while meeting key requirements for quality, integration, security, and governance.Gemini provides that connected foundation across the enterprise, and it’s why we b
entries.content:
Jamie de Guerre

Senior Director, Outbound Product Management

As organizations work to leverage AI to transform their businesses, it is clear that the raw model intelligence is not the key challenge.

Consistently, we hear that the challenges lie in how the agents can be deployed across the company while meeting key requirements for quality, integration, security, and governance.

Gemini provides that connected foundation across the enterprise, and it’s why we believe Google was named a Leader in the inaugural IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment1.

IDC MarketScape vendor analysis model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and suppliers in a given market. The research methodology utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier’s position within a given market. The Capabilities score measures supplier product, go-to-market and business execution in the short-term. The Strategy score measures alignment of supplier strategies with customer requirements in a 3-5 year timeframe. Supplier market share is represented by the size of the icons.

Gemini meets work where it already happens

A viable agentic platform has to meet work where it already happens – and run under production-grade controls. Gemini is engineered to deliver developer velocity without compromising governance, built around four core differentiators:

1. Surfaces that connect builders and business teams

Gemini makes it so that every surface connects back to one universal foundation.

  • Where teams already work: Employees collaborate with Gemini directly inside Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or team chats – the agent carries the same persistent memory, skills, and enterprise permissions across desktop and mobile without needing to switch tools.
  • Builder tools centered on choice: Gemini platform supports how developers want to work, spanning no-code and low-code builders in the studio to code-first workflows with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and Antigravity.
  • Workflows that compound across the organization: When a team solves a complex workflow, they can package it into a shared skill published to a central Agent Registry. Gemini calls on these skills directly to execute tasks, turning proven procedures into reusable assets across the entire company.

2. Radical openness across models, enterprise data, and tools

Gemini adapts to the software you already run, not the other way around.

  • Model choice: Through Model Garden in Gemini platform, teams have direct access to over 200 models – including all of the breakthroughs from Google DeepMind like Gemini 4 Argon, day one access to the latest Anthropic models, and third-party and open models.
  • Grounding on your enterprise data: Gemini connects directly to live enterprise data across Google Cloud in BigQuery and Cloud Storage, as well as Salesforce, SAP, and others. Because Gemini inherits each employee's existing credentials, sensitive information stays governed at the source.
  • Open standards: Built on open protocols like MCP and A2A, Gemini can easily plug into your existing toolchains and communicate across multi-vendor environments.

3. Smarter token economics

Gemini optimizes cost, latency, and performance directly at the execution layer.

  • Matching tasks to the right model: By default, Gemini uses Auto mode for users, letting the platform match each step of a task to the right model dynamically. It defaults to a fast workhorse model like Gemini Flash, and escalates to a high-capacity frontier reasoning model only when task complexity requires it.
  • Reusable skills: Teams can package proven processes into shared skills. Your agents can execute against these established procedures, improving consistency and reducing repetitive token consumption across the company.
  • Budget guardrails: Administrators can set spending limits by project, department, or individual agent in the billing console. When a budget threshold is reached, new requests pause while active tasks are allowed to complete, giving finance and engineering predictable cost controls without abruptly interrupting in-progress work.

4. Built-in governance and security

Gemini incorporates enterprise governance natively, and at no additional cost.

  • Dedicated agent identity: Every agent receives its own distinct, authenticated identity governed by least-privilege permissions. When an agent takes action, every event is recorded in an audit trail tied directly to that identity and the identity of which user was using the agent for the task.
  • Isolated sandboxes: A sandboxed boundary keeps dynamic tasks strictly contained, protecting your underlying infrastructure, core network, and sensitive corporate data from being exposed or compromised.
  • Policy enforcement: Rather than relying on a model to self-police, Agent Gateway automatically applies corporate security policies, blocks data leakage, and ensures agents only access what they are explicitly authorized to touch.

Looking forward

At its core, Gemini is all about giving your organization an open, reliable platform where builders have choice and teams work with complete confidence.

We are honored by IDC MarketScape’s recognition of Google as a Leader, and we look forward to continuing this work alongside our customers.

Download the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment excerpt to learn why Google is named a Leader.

1. SOURCE: “Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment”, October 2026, IDC # US54140926.

entries.title: Day 0 support for Reflection’s Beam on Google Cloud: 5x faster perf with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo
entries.summary: Today, Reflection released Beam, its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by
entries.content:
Injae Kwak

AI Infrastructure Product Manager

Shivaji Dutta

AI Infra Solutions Architect

Today, Reflection released Beam, its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models.

Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud:

"By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." - Joe Spisak, VP of Product & Head of Open Source, Reflection

With today’s day 0 release on Google Cloud, developers get:

  • Compounding model and system efficiency: Combining Beam’s 3x to 4x reasoning compute efficiency with system-level optimizations on A4X Max instances (NVIDIA GB300 NVL72) for up to 5x higher throughput and 8x lower latency,* and G4 VMs (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) for up to 2x higher throughput and 8x lower latency.*

  • High-efficiency multi-turn serving: KV-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and hierarchical KV cache offloading to Host DRAM and Local SSD reduce redundant prompt recomputation across long coding sessions.

  • Turnkey optimized deployment: Our recommended performance optimized recipes for agentic workloads with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo are available in AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes, llm-d repo and Model Garden in Gemini platformwith a few clicks. 

*Based on customer benchmarking

Scaling inference requires system-level optimization

When evaluating models for agentic coding and tool use, inference efficiency happens at two distinct layers: how efficiently the model reasons and how efficiently the serving system executes multi-turn loops.

Model-level efficiency: Reflection’s Beam

Reflection designed Beam (~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M-token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks.

Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step.

System-level efficiency: AI Hypercomputer optimized serving

Once developers deploy an agent into production, a second set of bottlenecks could appear at the serving layer. In an agentic coding loop, the model is called dozens of times in a single session. With every turn, the coding harness appends new file reads, code diffs, compiler logs, and tool outputs to a shared conversation history that quickly grows to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Even when the model itself generates 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens on each turn, the accumulated context window across turns creates two major infrastructure challenges:

First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck. Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users.

Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity. Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls.

To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang).

Inside the AI Hypercomputer inference architecture

To run Beam’s BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle.

System optimized architecture for serving agentic traffic

Rather than treating inference pods as stateless endpoints, each layer of the stack is co-designed around the multi-turn agent lifecycle:

  • Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control.

  • Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance): Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation.

  • Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory (Tier 1), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs (Tier 2) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch.

System optimizations for multi-turn agentic workloads

When serving multi-turn coding and tool-use workloads like the AgentX trajectory dataset across rising concurrency levels, each layer in the serving stack contributes to the performance and latency improvements for multi-turn, long context traffic patterns of agentic workloads:

A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure.

NVIDIA Dynamo optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam

llm-d optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam

Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously:

  • Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales.

  • KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput.

  • Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity.

  • Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast.
